subject: sociology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

options: Lacking the minimum needed to survive, such as food, shelter and clothing
Being poorer than most people in your society
questions.explain: Absolute poverty means lacking the basic essentials needed for survival.

options: Only when unable to survive at all
Compared with the general standard of living in one's society
questions.explain: Relative poverty is measured against the typical standard of living in a particular society.

options: Random opportunities given by the government
A person's luck in games of chance
The number of years someone lives
A person's likelihood of obtaining things society values, like health, education and wealth
questions.explain: Life chances are the opportunities (or lack of them) people have to obtain valued things like good health, education and income.

questions.q: The functionalist theory of stratification by Davis and Moore argues that inequality is:
options: Necessary and functional because it motivates the most able to fill important roles
Caused only by the ruling class
A myth that does not exist
questions.explain: Davis and Moore argued unequal rewards are functional, ensuring the most able people are motivated to take society's important roles.

questions.q: The 'culture of poverty' explanation argues that poverty is partly caused by:
options: A set of values and attitudes (e.g. fatalism) passed on among the poor
A complete lack of any wealthy people
questions.explain: The culture of poverty thesis (Oscar Lewis) suggests some poor groups develop values, like fatalism, that help reproduce poverty.

options: The amount of money someone has only
The social position or honour attached to a person or role
questions.explain: Status refers to the social position and prestige attached to a person or role, which can differ from wealth.

questions.q: In sociology, the difference between 'wealth' and 'income' is that:
options: Wealth is the total value of assets owned; income is money received regularly (e.g. wages)
Income is always larger than wealth
questions.explain: Wealth is the stock of assets a person owns, while income is the flow of money received, such as wages or benefits.

options: Fixed at birth or given regardless of effort (e.g. inherited title)
questions.explain: Ascribed status is fixed at birth or assigned independent of a person's efforts, unlike achieved status.

questions.q: The Marxist view of stratification argues that the main divide in capitalist society is between:
questions.explain: Marx argued society is divided by ownership of the means of production into the bourgeoisie and the proletariat.

questions.q: Which statement about the gender pay gap is most accurate?
options: Women on average still tend to earn less than men over their careers
Men and women have always earned exactly the same
The gap was abolished in the 1900s
questions.explain: On average women still tend to earn less than men, reflecting ongoing gender inequality in pay.

questions.q: A 'meritocracy' is a society in which positions are supposedly allocated according to:
questions.explain: In a meritocracy, rewards and positions are based on talent and effort rather than birth.

options: Movement of people between different positions in the class structure
Moving house to a new town
questions.explain: Social mobility is movement up or down the social hierarchy between classes or positions.
